summary: Ivan Burazin of Daytona presents the thesis that agent experience (AX) is the successor to developer experience, arguing that building devtools for humans is now building for the past. He cites YC data: 25% of startups report AI writes 95% of their code, and 37% of the latest batch build agents as their product. He predicts agent populations will grow exponentially relative to humans. The core uncomfortable truth is that most existing tools break the moment a human is removed from the loop. Burazin adopts the AX definition from Shaun at Netifi—how easily agents can access, understand, and operate within digital environments—but adds the critical word 'autonomously,' arguing that if an agent must fall back to a human, the tool is not truly agent-native. He surveys early AX implementers: Arcade for seamless authentication with human fallback, Stripe for agent-readable docs (append .md to any doc URL), the llms.txt standard, and API-first design exemplified by Neon, Netifi, and Supabase. Burazin then details Daytona's agent-native runtime sandboxes: 27ms spin-up, full API control, and preloaded headless tools (file explorer, git client, LSP, terminal). As users pushed agents further, Daytona discovered new primitives for full autonomy. The first is a declarative image builder where agents declare requirements and Daytona builds images on the fly, avoiding brittle Docker builds. The second is Daytona volumes: shared datasets mountable as network drives across all environments, solving the problem of agents repeatedly downloading large (e.g., 100GB) datasets. The third is parallel execution: agents can fork a machine thousands of times and try approaches simultaneously, unlike humans limited to one or two machines. Burazin candidly admits that what else AX requires is still being discovered as people build agents. He closes by noting Daytona initially invested heavily in terminal/CLI DX but pivoted to prioritize agent-first design, warning that if agents can't use your product end-to-end, no one will.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The Agent Future and AX Definition
sections.summary: Burazin opens with agent population growth (humans to the power of n), YC data points on AI code generation and agent products, and the uncomfortable truth that most tools break without humans. He introduces Agent Experience (AX), coined by Matt at Netifi and defined by Shaun, as how easily agents can access, understand, and operate within digital environments.

sections.title: AX Implementation Examples
sections.summary: Surveys companies implementing AX: Arcade for seamless authentication with human fallback, Stripe for agent-readable docs (.md URLs), the llms.txt standard, and API-first design from Neon, Netifi, and Supabase. Emphasizes API as the essential machine-native interface, noting MCP discussion but focusing on underlying API technology.

sections.title: The Autonomy Dimension
sections.summary: Burazin adds 'autonomously' to Shaun's AX definition, arguing tools requiring human fallback are not future-proof. Mentions Swix challenged him that AX is just wrapped DX, motivating the autonomy focus. Without solving for full autonomy, builders are porting the past.

sections.title: Speaker Background and Daytona Introduction
sections.summary: Burazin recounts his history: building data centers, creating the first browser-based IDE in 2009, leading developer experience at Infobip, and now co-founding Daytona—an agent-native runtime providing sandboxes for AI-generated code, described as what a laptop is to a human.

sections.title: Daytona's AX Features and New Primitives
sections.summary: Details Daytona's initial AX features: 27ms spin-up, API-first control, and preloaded headless tools. Then introduces the declarative image builder: agents declare requirements and Daytona builds the image on the fly, avoiding brittle autonomous Docker builds.

sections.title: Volumes, Parallel Execution, and Closing
sections.summary: Introduces Daytona volumes for sharing large datasets across isolated environments via network-mounted drives, eliminating repeated downloads. Describes parallel execution as a unique agent capability: forking a machine thousands of times to try approaches simultaneously. Burazin admits what else AX needs is still being discovered. He closes by noting Daytona pivoted from terminal/CLI DX investment to agent-first focus, warning that if agents can't use your product end-to-end, no one will. Daytona is open source on GitHub.

demonstrations: Stripe agent-readable docs: appending .md to any doc URL returns clean markdown
Arcade authentication flow: agent attempts login, falls back to user, then proceeds autonomously
Daytona declarative image builder: agent specifies base image and dependencies, environment built on the fly
Daytona volumes: agent uploads a dataset once, mounts it as a network drive on every environment
Parallel execution: agent forks a machine multiple times to try approaches simultaneously rather than sequentially
limitations: Most existing devtools break when a human is removed from the loop
Agents parsing terminal output is suboptimal
Agents building Docker images autonomously is brittle, slow, and breaks often
Isolated environments force agents to re-download large datasets each time without shared volumes
Sequential trial-and-error is inefficient compared to parallel execution agents can perform
What AX fully requires is still unknown and being discovered incrementally
No comprehensive data exists on agent population growth
